steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper introducing KGQuiz, a benchmark for evaluating how well the knowledge encoded in large language models generalizes across task formats and knowledge domains. Cover the motivation, the gaps in existing knowledge probing work, the benchmark design, and our main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs encode knowledge, but their knowledge abilities are brittle
2. Existing probing studies and benchmarks
3. Gap 1: Knowledge Utilization
4. Gap 2: Knowledge Breadth
5. KGQuiz: design and tasks
6. Evaluation and findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLM knowledge
- LLMs encode real-world knowledge in parameters; advance knowledge-intensive tasks: open-domain QA, dialogue generation, summarization, more
- but brittle: hallucinated information, struggle with long-tail facts, fail to abstain when info not in parameters

2. Existing work
- studies + benchmarks probe LLM knowledge
- later: temporality, time-sensitive facts
- knowledge-intensive tasks also used to evaluate: open-domain QA, fact-checking, more
- two important but underexplored factors

3. Knowledge Utilization
- previous works: limited formats like fill-in-the-blank
- task complexity/format may influence knowledge abilities; often unaddressed
- e.g. factual editing: identify factual inconsistency + correct, not just memorization
- reasoning with structured knowledge: model knowledge in networks/graphs, not only atomic level
- how well abilities generalize to tasks/contexts of varying format + complexity: underexplored

4. Knowledge Breadth
- existing works mostly Wikipedia or one domain like biomedical
- LLM performance varies significantly across domains; not adequately addressed
- lack of multi-domain evaluation (diverse sources, subject areas) hinders comprehensive understanding

5. KGQuiz
- comprehensive benchmark; multiple knowledge utilization patterns, diverse domains
- built from structured info in knowledge graphs (KGs) from three domains: commonsense, encyclopedic, domain-specific (biomedical)
- per KG: 41,000 knowledge-intensive questions
- five tasks of increasing complexity: true-or-false, multiple choice, blank-filling, multi-hop factual editing, open-ended text generation
- test: judging factual correctness, selecting facts based on model confidence, retrieving entities, factual editing, generating long-form knowledge documents -> holistic probe

6. Findings
- 10 open-source and black-box LLMs evaluated
- 1) performance varies greatly across domains; Task 5 Open-Ended Text Generation: ChatGPT best on YAGO, ChatGLM on ConceptNet, text-davinci-003 on UMLS
- 2) knowledge utilization strongly affects retrieving/using facts; ChatGPT on biomedical drops 30% from fill-in-the-blank to factual editing -> multi-hop context is a new challenge
- probing is nuanced + multi-faceted; largest LLMs excel at simple tasks on general domains; advanced contexts + domain-specific info still open
- KGQuiz pinpoints strengths + limitations by task and domain; testbed to understand, evaluate, improve LLM knowledge

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown incredible abilities to encode and represent real-world knowledge in their model parameters, and this has advanced knowledge-intensive tasks such as open-domain question answering, dialogue generation, summarization, and more. But their knowledge abilities can also be quite brittle: LLMs generate hallucinated information, they struggle to encode long-tail facts, and they fall short of abstaining when the relevant information is not in the model parameters.

Because of this, studies and benchmarks have been proposed to probe the knowledge abilities of LLMs. Later works also looked at temporality, evaluating whether LLMs can handle time-sensitive facts and information. Besides just probing LLM knowledge, knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain QA, fact-checking, and more are also proposed and used to evaluate LLM knowledge abilities. These works contributed to understanding and expanding the stored knowledge of large language models, but we find two important factors in LLM knowledge abilities that are still underexplored.

Knowledge Utilization: Previous works have mostly focused on limited task formats like fill-in-the-blank questions to test the model's knowledge abilities. But the complexity or format of a task might influence a model's knowledge abilities, and this important aspect is often not addressed in the current literature. For example, factual editing requires the model to identify factual inconsistency and make corrections, instead of just evaluating memorization; reasoning with structured knowledge looks at the model's ability to model knowledge in networks and graphs, instead of only probing knowledge at the atomic level. So how well LLM knowledge abilities generalize to tasks and contexts with different format and complexity is still underexplored.

Knowledge Breadth: Existing works mostly use Wikipedia or a specific domain like biomedical knowledge as the knowledge source for evaluation. But it has been observed that LLM performance can vary a lot across different knowledge domains, and this has not been addressed enough in the previous works of LLM knowledge probing and understanding. So there is no multi-domain knowledge evaluation of large language models that covers diverse knowledge sources, subject areas, and more, and this is hindering a comprehensive understanding of LLM knowledge abilities.

- KGQuiz
  - benchmark across knowledge utilization patterns + diverse domains
  - built from KGs in three domains: commonsense, encyclopedic, domain-specific (biomedical)
  - 41,000 questions per KG; five tasks of increasing complexity: true-or-false, multiple choice, blank-filling, multi-hop factual editing, open-ended text generation
  - tests judging correctness, selecting facts by confidence, retrieving entities, factual editing, long-form generation
- Findings
  - 10 open-source + black-box LLMs
  - domains vary: Task 5, ChatGPT best on YAGO, ChatGLM on ConceptNet, text-davinci-003 on UMLS
  - utilization matters: ChatGPT biomedical drops 30% from fill-in-the-blank to factual editing
  - largest LLMs good at simple tasks on general domains; advanced contexts + domain-specific still open
  - KGQuiz as testbed

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown incredible abilities to encode and represent real-world knowledge in their model parameters, and this has advanced knowledge-intensive tasks such as open-domain question answering, dialogue generation, summarization, and more. But their knowledge abilities can also be quite brittle: LLMs generate hallucinated information, they struggle to encode long-tail facts, and they fall short of abstaining when the relevant information is not in the model parameters.

Because of this, studies and benchmarks have been proposed to probe the knowledge abilities of LLMs. Later works also looked at temporality, evaluating whether LLMs can handle time-sensitive facts and information. Besides just probing LLM knowledge, knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain QA, fact-checking, and more are also proposed and used to evaluate LLM knowledge abilities. These works contributed to understanding and expanding the stored knowledge of large language models, but we find two important factors in LLM knowledge abilities that are still underexplored.

Knowledge Utilization: Previous works have mostly focused on limited task formats like fill-in-the-blank questions to test the model's knowledge abilities. But the complexity or format of a task might influence a model's knowledge abilities, and this important aspect is often not addressed in the current literature. For example, factual editing requires the model to identify factual inconsistency and make corrections, instead of just evaluating memorization; reasoning with structured knowledge looks at the model's ability to model knowledge in networks and graphs, instead of only probing knowledge at the atomic level. So how well LLM knowledge abilities generalize to tasks and contexts with different format and complexity is still underexplored.

Knowledge Breadth: Existing works mostly use Wikipedia or a specific domain like biomedical knowledge as the knowledge source for evaluation. But it has been observed that LLM performance can vary a lot across different knowledge domains, and this has not been addressed enough in the previous works of LLM knowledge probing and understanding. So there is no multi-domain knowledge evaluation of large language models that covers diverse knowledge sources, subject areas, and more, and this is hindering a comprehensive understanding of LLM knowledge abilities.

For this, we propose KGQuiz, a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate the knowledge abilities of large language models across multiple knowledge utilization patterns in diverse knowledge domains. The KGQuiz benchmark is built with structured information from knowledge graphs (KGs) from three different domains, which represent commonsense, encyclopedic, and domain-specific (biomedical) knowledge. For each knowledge graph, KGQuiz has a collection of 41,000 knowledge-intensive questions that cover five tasks of increasing complexity: true-or-false, multiple choice, blank-filling, multi-hop factual editing, and open-ended text generation. These tasks get progressively more difficult and they represent the many LLM knowledge and reasoning abilities, which gives a comprehensive and comparative setting to assess LLMs' abilities. They test LLMs' abilities to judge factual correctness, to select facts based on model confidence, to retrieve entities, to perform factual editing, and to generate long-form knowledge documents, so together they are a holistic probe of LLM knowledge abilities in different application scenarios.

We evaluate 10 open-source and black-box large language models on the KGQuiz benchmark to better understand which LLM covers which knowledge domain better, and in which utilization contexts. Our experiments show that: 1) LLM performance varies a lot across knowledge domains. For example, on Task 5: Open-Ended Text Generation, ChatGPT, ChatGLM, and text-davinci-003 perform best on YAGO, ConceptNet, and UMLS respectively, which are three knowledge graphs representing different knowledge domains. 2) Knowledge utilization has a big impact on LLM's ability to retrieve and use factual knowledge. For example, ChatGPT's performance on biomedical knowledge drops by 30% from the fill-in-the-blank task to the factual editing task, which suggests that the additional multi-hop context in factual editing creates new challenges for LLM knowledge abilities. Overall, our experiments show that probing the knowledge abilities of LLMs is nuanced and multi-faceted. The largest LLMs do very well on simple knowledge utilization tasks on general knowledge domains, while advanced knowledge contexts and domain-specific information are still open challenges. KGQuiz helps to pinpoint the strengths and knowledge limitations of LLMs with respect to tasks and domains. We see KGQuiz as a valuable testbed to understand, evaluate, and improve LLM knowledge abilities across different knowledge domains and utilization contexts.

steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated incredible abilities to encode and represent real-world knowledge in their model parameters, advancing knowledge-intensive tasks such as open-domain question answering [1,2,3,4,5,6], dialogue generation [7,8,9], summarization [10,11,12], and more. However, their knowledge abilities can also be quite brittle, with LLMs generating hallucinated information [13,14,15,16,17], struggling to encode long-tail facts [15], and failing to abstain when relevant information is not present in model parameters [18].

As a result, studies and benchmarks have been proposed to probe the knowledge abilities of LLMs [19,20,21,22,23,24]. Later works also examined temporality, evaluating whether LLMs could handle time-sensitive facts and information [20]. Beyond merely probing LLM knowledge, knowledge-intensive tasks such as open-domain QA [25,26,27], fact-checking [28,29,27], and more have also been proposed and used to evaluate LLM knowledge abilities. Despite these works’ contributions to understanding and expanding the stored knowledge of large language models, we identify two important yet underexplored factors in LLM knowledge abilities.

Knowledge Utilization: Previous works have primarily focused on limited task formats such as fill-in-the-blank questions to test the model’s knowledge abilities [19,30,31]. However, the complexity or format of a task might influence a model’s knowledge abilities, an aspect that often goes unaddressed in the current literature. For example, factual editing [32,33] requires the model to identify factual inconsistency and make corrections, rather than simply evaluating memorization; reasoning with structured knowledge [34,35] examines the model’s ability to model knowledge in networks and graphs, instead of only probing knowledge at the atomic level. How well LLM knowledge abilities generalize to tasks and contexts of varying format and complexity therefore remains underexplored.

Knowledge Breadth: Existing works predominantly use Wikipedia or a specific domain like biomedical knowledge as the knowledge source for evaluation. However, LLM performance has been observed to vary significantly across knowledge domains [23,22], an aspect not adequately addressed in previous work on LLM knowledge probing and understanding. The lack of a multi-domain knowledge evaluation of large language models, covering diverse knowledge sources, subject areas, and more, is thus hindering a comprehensive understanding of LLM knowledge abilities.

To this end, we propose KGQuiz, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the knowledge abilities of large language models across multiple knowledge utilization patterns in diverse knowledge domains. The KGQuiz benchmark is constructed with structured information from knowledge graphs (KGs) from three different domains, representing commonsense, encyclopedic, and domain-specific (biomedical) knowledge. For each knowledge graph, KGQuiz presents a collection of 41,000 knowledge-intensive questions covering five tasks of increasing complexity: true-or-false, multiple choice, blank-filling, multi-hop factual editing, and open-ended text generation. These progressively difficult tasks represent the many facets of LLM knowledge and reasoning abilities and provide a comprehensive and comparative setting to assess LLMs: they respectively test LLMs’ abilities to judge factual correctness, select facts based on model confidence, retrieve entities, perform factual editing, and generate long-form knowledge documents, together forming a holistic probe of LLM knowledge abilities in different application scenarios.

We evaluate 10 open-source and black-box large language models on the KGQuiz benchmark to better understand which LLM covers which knowledge domain better, and under which utilization contexts. Our experiments demonstrate that: 1) LLM performance varies greatly across knowledge domains. For instance, on Task 5: Open-Ended Text Generation, ChatGPT [36], ChatGLM [37], and text-davinci-003 [36] respectively perform best on YAGO, ConceptNet, and UMLS, three knowledge graphs representing different knowledge domains. 2) Knowledge utilization greatly impacts LLMs’ ability to retrieve and use factual knowledge. For instance, ChatGPT’s performance on biomedical knowledge drops by 30% from the fill-in-the-blank task to the factual editing task, suggesting that the additional multi-hop context in factual editing poses new challenges to LLM knowledge abilities. Together, our experiments demonstrate that probing the knowledge abilities of LLMs is nuanced and multi-faceted: the largest LLMs excel at simple knowledge utilization tasks on general knowledge domains, while advanced knowledge contexts and domain-specific information remain open challenges. KGQuiz helps pinpoint the strengths and knowledge limitations of LLMs with respect to tasks and domains. We envision KGQuiz as a valuable testbed to understand, evaluate, and improve LLM knowledge abilities across varying knowledge domains and utilization contexts.
